title: Design chat and presence
summary: Millions of open WebSockets: connection gateways, per-conversation sequence numbers, receipts, offline delivery, many devices per user, and presence from heartbeats with a TTL.

steps.title: Requirements and estimates
body: **The ask:** one-to-one and small group chat (up to a few hundred members), on phones and laptops at once, with
"online" dots and sent / delivered / read ticks.
| Kind | Requirement |
| Functional | send and receive; history; receipts; presence; offline users get a push and catch up on open |
| Non-functional | delivery under ~500 ms when online; **never lose** a message once acked; per-conversation order; history kept for years |
| Out of scope | end-to-end encryption key exchange (mention it changes what the server can see), voice and video, huge broadcast channels |
```text
users         50 M daily active, 10 M connected at peak
messages      40 / user / day = 2 B / day   ≈ 23,000 / s average, ~70,000 / s peak
storage       2 B x ~200 bytes = 400 GB / day  ≈ 146 TB / year before replication
connections   10 M long-lived WebSockets, mostly idle
The unusual number is the last one: the hard part is **holding 10 M connections** and knowing which machine
holds whose, not the message rate.

steps.prompt: Each gateway node holds 100,000 idle WebSockets comfortably. You run in 3 availability zones and must survive losing one zone at peak (10 M connections). How many gateway nodes?
steps.explain: 10 M / 100k = 100 nodes. If one of 3 zones dies, the other two must hold everything, so each zone needs 50 nodes: 150 in total. When a zone dies, 3.3 M clients reconnect at once: reconnect with jittered backoff or the survivors are hit by a stampede.

steps.title: The high-level design
body: ```text
\      /   WebSocket (TLS)                           | session registry |
| gateway nodes  |<-->| chat service        |-------->| (Redis, TTL)     |
| hold sockets   |    | owns conversations, |         +------------------+
+----------------+    | assigns seq numbers |
| message store       |  partitioned by conversation_id
| (conv_id, seq) PK   |
- **Gateways** only hold sockets and forward frames. They are stateless apart from the sockets, so a deploy
drains them gradually.
- The **session registry** maps each user to the gateways where their devices are connected, with a TTL so dead
entries vanish.
- The **message store** is keyed by `(conversation_id, seq)`: reading history and "everything after seq 41" are
range scans on one partition. A wide-column or key-value store with range keys fits well.

steps.prompt: Put the path of one message in order.
lines: The phone sends the message with a client message id over its WebSocket
The gateway forwards it to the chat service instance that owns the conversation
The chat service assigns the next sequence number and stores the message durably
It acks the sender with the sequence number, then pushes the message to each member's gateways from the registry
Members with no live connection get a push notification that wakes the app to sync
steps.explain: Store before you ack: an ack promises the message survives. The client message id makes a resend after a lost ack harmless: the service sees the same id and returns the same seq.

steps.title: Ordering: one writer per conversation
body: Clocks on phones are wrong and messages race over different paths, so timestamps cannot order a conversation.
Give each conversation **one writer** (route by `conversation_id` to one partition or one service instance) and
let it hand out **sequence numbers** 1, 2, 3, ...
Clients use them two ways:
- **Dedupe and order:** show messages sorted by seq; ignore a seq already shown.
- **Gap detection:** a client that last saw 41 and receives 42, 43, 46 knows 44 and 45 are missing and fetches
`after=43` from the store. The push channel can lose frames; the store cannot.
Order is only promised **inside** a conversation. Across conversations nobody can tell, so do not pay for it.

steps.prompt: A client last saw seq 41. What does this print?
code: for (var s = lastSeen + 1; s <= max; s++)
steps.explain: 44 arrived out of order, so it is not missing. Only 45 is, and the client asks the store for it.

steps.title: Receipts, offline delivery and many devices
body: - **Receipts are numbers, not flags.** Store per member the highest seq *delivered* and the highest seq *read*.
"Read up to 57" covers every message before it, so one small write replaces dozens.
- **Offline delivery is a sync, not a queue.** The push notification says "something new"; the app then
connects and asks for everything after its last seq. Push payloads can be dropped or delayed, so never put
the only copy of a message in one.
- **Each device has its own cursor.** The phone may be at seq 57 and the laptop at 40. Fan out to every
connected device of each member; each catches up from its own position.
- **Groups** multiply fan-out by members: a 500-member group turns one message into 500 deliveries. Very large
channels switch to pull (clients fetch), like celebrity feeds.

steps.prompt: Match each mechanism to the problem it solves.
pairs: A resend after a lost ack does not create a duplicate
Everyone sees the same order, and gaps are detectable
One write marks many messages as read
Finding which gateways hold a user's devices
Offline devices catch up even if a push was dropped

steps.title: Presence: heartbeats and a TTL
body: A socket can die without a goodbye (a phone enters a tunnel). So presence is a **lease**:
```text
device sends heartbeat every 30 s   ->   presence key   last_seen = now,  TTL 90 s
no heartbeat for 90 s               ->   key expires     ->   offline
- Make the TTL **2-3 x the heartbeat interval**, so one late or lost heartbeat does not flip the dot.
- A user is online if **any** device is.
- Do not broadcast every change to every contact: 10 M users with 200 contacts each is billions of events.
Push changes only to people who are looking (an open chat or contact list), and let others fetch on demand.
- Debounce flaps: show "offline" only after it has lasted a few seconds.

prompt: **Symptom first.** Users complain their friends' dots flicker between online and offline every minute or so.
Config:
```yaml
presence:
heartbeatIntervalSeconds: 30
ttlSeconds: 30
What is the cause?
options: The TTL equals the heartbeat interval, so any heartbeat that is a little late lets the key expire. Make the TTL 2-3 x the interval
The heartbeat is too slow: send one every second
The session registry is out of memory and evicting keys
WebSockets cannot carry heartbeats; use HTTP polling
steps.explain: Network jitter, a GC pause or a busy phone delays heartbeats by a second or two all the time. With TTL = interval there is no margin. Heartbeating every second would multiply the load 30 times for no gain.

steps.title: A presence tracker
prompt: Write a class `PresenceTracker` with time passed in:
- `PresenceTracker(long ttlMs)`.
- `void Heartbeat(string user, string device, long nowMs)`: that device was seen now.
- `void Disconnect(string user, string device)`: a clean goodbye; the device stops counting at once.
- `bool IsOnline(string user, long nowMs)`: true when **any** of the user's devices was seen less than `ttlMs`
ago (`nowMs - lastSeen < ttlMs`).
- `List<string> Online(long nowMs)`: every online user, sorted with ordinal string order.
starter: public void Heartbeat(string user, string device, long nowMs) { }
public void Disconnect(string user, string device) { }
public bool IsOnline(string user, long nowMs) => false;
solution: readonly Dictionary<string, Dictionary<string, long>> seen = new();
public void Heartbeat(string user, string device, long nowMs)
if (!seen.TryGetValue(user, out var devices)) seen[user] = devices = new();
public void Disconnect(string user, string device)
public bool IsOnline(string user, long nowMs) =>
seen.TryGetValue(user, out var devices) && devices.Values.Any(t => nowMs - t < ttlMs);
hints: Keep `Dictionary<string, Dictionary<string, long>>`: user -> device -> last seen.
template: var dojoP = new PresenceTracker(90_000);
dojoP.Heartbeat("ana", "phone", 0);
Dojo.Eq("online just inside the TTL", true, dojoP.IsOnline("ana", 89_999));
Dojo.Eq("offline once the TTL has passed", false, dojoP.IsOnline("ana", 90_000));
dojoP.Heartbeat("ana", "laptop", 60_000);
Dojo.Eq("online while any device is", true, dojoP.IsOnline("ana", 100_000));
dojoP.Disconnect("ana", "laptop");
Dojo.Eq("a clean disconnect counts at once", false, dojoP.IsOnline("ana", 100_000));
Dojo.Eq("unknown users are offline", false, dojoP.IsOnline("zed", 0));
dojoP.Heartbeat("cy", "phone", 95_000);
dojoP.Heartbeat("bo", "phone", 50_000);
Dojo.Eq("who is online at 120 s", new List<string> { "bo", "cy" }, dojoP.Online(120_000));
Dojo.Eq("nobody at 500 s", new List<string>(), dojoP.Online(500_000));

steps.title: Sequence numbers and gaps
prompt: Write a class `ConversationLog`, the single writer of each conversation:
- `long Append(string conversation, string clientMessageId)`: gives the message the next sequence number of its
conversation (the first is `1`) and returns it. If the same conversation already has this client message id,
return its existing number and do **not** use up a new one (a retried send).
- `static List<long> Missing(long lastSeen, IEnumerable<long> received)`: the numbers after `lastSeen` and up to
the largest received one that did not arrive, ascending. Numbers at or below `lastSeen` are ignored.
starter: public long Append(string conversation, string clientMessageId) => 0;
public static List<long> Missing(long lastSeen, IEnumerable<long> received) => new();
solution: readonly Dictionary<(string Conversation, string ClientId), long> byClientId = new();
public long Append(string conversation, string clientMessageId)
if (byClientId.TryGetValue((conversation, clientMessageId), out var existing)) return existing;
public static List<long> Missing(long lastSeen, IEnumerable<long> received)
var max = got.Count == 0 ? lastSeen : Math.Max(lastSeen, got.Max());
for (var s = lastSeen + 1; s <= max; s++)
hints: Two dictionaries: conversation -> last seq, and (conversation, client id) -> seq.
For `Missing`, put the received numbers in a `HashSet<long>` and walk from `lastSeen + 1` to the largest one.
template: var dojoC = new ConversationLog();
Dojo.Eq("first message is 1", 1L, dojoC.Append("c1", "m1"));
Dojo.Eq("second message is 2", 2L, dojoC.Append("c1", "m2"));
Dojo.Eq("each conversation counts on its own", 1L, dojoC.Append("c2", "x1"));
Dojo.Eq("a retried send keeps its number", 1L, dojoC.Append("c1", "m1"));
Dojo.Eq("and does not use one up", 3L, dojoC.Append("c1", "m3"));
Dojo.Eq("the same client id in another conversation is a new message", 2L, dojoC.Append("c2", "m1"));
Dojo.Eq("one gap", new List<long> { 45 }, ConversationLog.Missing(41, new long[] { 42, 43, 46, 44 }));
Dojo.Eq("several gaps", new List<long> { 2, 3, 4 }, ConversationLog.Missing(0, new long[] { 5, 1, 5 }));
Dojo.Eq("old numbers are ignored", new List<long>(), ConversationLog.Missing(3, new long[] { 3, 2 }));
Dojo.Eq("nothing received, nothing known to be missing", new List<long>(), ConversationLog.Missing(5, new long[0]));
